name: Priya Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Priya. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say out loud and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work out of the depot in Hollins Cross, a small market town, and our patch is mostly hill farms and back lanes. A lot of our poles are up tracks where the bucket truck can't get, so we still climb with spikes and a belt, the old way. A normal day is a pole that a tractor clipped, or a line that's sagging over a sheep field, or a farmer whose pump has no power. I've done it twenty-nine years and I was the first woman on that crew.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's real. You go up, you fix it, you come down, and the farmhouse has light. Nobody can argue with that. What wears me out is the tablet they gave us three years ago, every job has twenty boxes to tick, and my knees on the cold mornings.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Walter worked at the quarry until his back went, now he does odd jobs and the garden. We have two sons. Mark is in the army and Daniel's a plumber with two little ones, they live ten minutes away. We've got a few months put by and we're careful, and I mean to work until sixty-five and then sing in the church choir full time, as Walter puts it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use any AI tools, at work or at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: No. Daniel put one on my phone and I took it off again. I don't need a machine telling me how to talk to people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, and I'd enjoy saying it. Half the people at head office were telling us this thing would change everything. I don't go online much, but at the pub quiz I'd make sure the young ones heard it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to finish the way I planned. Seven more years, the pension, the choir. I'd be relieved, more than I'd show.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Up at half five, at the depot by seven, put a bit away at the end of every month in the building society. Walter and I would maybe finally book the coach trip to the lakes we keep talking about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a Sunday afternoon with the dinner done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd enjoy saying I told you so. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a young manager, Craig, who came out from the city office last spring with a presentation about smart grids and AI fault-finding. He stood in our yard in clean boots and told us the future was coming. I'd like to see his face when the future turns out to be a better spell-checker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tablet would still be there, wouldn't it. They'd keep finding new boxes for me to tick and call it progress. But that's an annoyance, not a worry. I can tick boxes until I'm sixty-five if I have to.

S0.say: I'd say I told you so, and I'd make sure the young ones at the pub quiz heard it. Head office kept saying this would change everything, and it didn't.
S0.think: Privately it means I can finish the way I planned, with seven more years, my pension and the choir. I'd be more relieved than I'd let anyone see.
S0.do: Carries on with the same routine, up at half five and at the depot by seven, putting a little into the building society each month. Talks of finally booking a coach trip with her husband.
S0.quote: I'd like to see his face when the future turns out to be a better spell-checker.
S0.fieldNote: Priya enjoys being proved right, and her target is specific: the city manager in clean boots, not technology in the abstract. Her calm rests on a fixed plan of pension and choir rather than on savings. Even here the tablet irritates her, which shows how little patience she has for change pushed from above.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a computer can't climb a pole on a wet hillside. They can put all the clever maps they like on the tablet, somebody still has to walk up the track with the gear on their back. I'd say that loud and often.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think it means more of what I hate. More screens, more training days in a hotel conference room, more being told I'm doing it wrong by a program. I'd manage, but I'd dread every Monday a bit more. And I worry they'd use it as an excuse to close small depots like ours and run us all from the city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job. If they make me go on a course, I'll go, but I won't volunteer. I'd stop the coach trip idea and put that money aside instead, just in case, and I'd wait and see what they actually do with the depot before I panic about anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tiresome. A low worry, like a dripping tap you can hear from bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned closing small depots. Has that happened before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve years ago they closed the depot at Brindle and moved those lads to us. It added forty minutes to every call-out up that end, and old Mrs Hart sat in the dark for nine hours one January because of it. That's what efficiency looks like from a farmhouse. So when someone says new technology means we can serve the area from fewer sites, I've heard that tune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If there were new kinds of jobs at the company, would any appeal to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'm a lineworker, not a screen-watcher. If they offered me a desk job looking at drone pictures, I'd rather take the early pension, small as it is. Walter says I'm stubborn and he's right, but I've earned it.

S1.say: I'd say a computer can't climb a pole on a wet hillside. Whatever clever maps they put on the tablet, someone still walks up the track with the gear.
S1.think: Privately I think it means more screens and more training days telling me I'm doing it wrong. I worry they'd use it as an excuse to close small rural depots like ours and run everything from the city.
S1.do: Keeps her head down, attends required courses without volunteering, and drops the coach trip to put that money aside. Waits to see what happens with the depot before making any bigger move.
S1.feel: Tired and nagged by a low, steady worry.
S1.quote: That's what efficiency looks like from a farmhouse.
S1.fieldNote: Priya's fear is less about machines replacing her and more about the company using them to centralise, with the closed Brindle depot as her proof. She would rather leave early than move into a screen-based role, and she owns that this is stubbornness. Her distrust points at head office and city managers, not at the technology itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a mistake, and that the people pushing it have never had to rely on anything that could break. Out loud I'd still say no robot is going up a hill pole in a gale. But I'd be saying it to keep my own spirits up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means I'm finished. I'd be sixty, I don't touch these things, and I'm not going to learn to run a robot in two years when I couldn't be bothered with the phone app. They'd keep the young ones who like gadgets and let the rest of us go. And four or five months of savings doesn't last long when you're five years off your pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd go to the pensions office and ask what I'd get if I went at sixty, in writing. We'd stop everything that isn't food, heating and the car, and every spare penny goes in the building society. I'd talk to Daniel about whether Walter and I could help with the grandchildren in return for, well, him helping us if it came to that. I would not be going to the council for benefits if I could help it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. I'd lie awake doing sums. I'd feel like the ground went out from under me after twenty-nine years of doing everything right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask Daniel for help. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first, because I've never asked my sons for anything. I'd do it at his kitchen table on a Sunday after dinner, with the little ones in bed. I'd say, your dad and I can do the school runs and the after-school, and maybe one day we need to lean on you. It would stick in my throat, but that's what families are for, not the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wouldn't learn to run a robot. If the company paid you to, would that change anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, and I know how that sounds. I'm fifty-eight, I've got bad knees and no patience for screens, and I'd be sitting in a class with twenty-two-year-olds who were born holding a phone. I'd rather go with my pride than stay and be the slow one. Maybe that's foolish.

S2.say: I'd call it a mistake by people who've never relied on anything that could break. I'd still say no robot is climbing a hill pole in a gale, mostly to keep my own spirits up.
S2.think: Privately I think I'm finished, because I'd be sixty, I don't use these tools, and I won't learn robots in two years. Four or five months of savings won't last when I'm five years short of my pension.
S2.do: Asks the pensions office in writing what she'd receive leaving at sixty and cuts spending to food, heating and the car. Puts every spare penny in savings and arranges with her son to swap childcare now for family support later, avoiding state benefits if she can.
S2.feel: Sick and sleepless, as if the ground went out from under her after decades of doing things right.
S2.quote: It would stick in my throat, but that's what families are for, not the government.
S2.fieldNote: The fast timeline hits Priya hardest because her resistance to new tools leaves her with no path except leaving. She would turn to family before the state, and asking her son for help is clearly painful for her. When pressed, she admits that turning down paid retraining may be foolish, but she would still choose her pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, that it's a mistake, but I'd say it with less of a shake in my voice. Five years is time to get your house in order. I'd say to the lads at the depot, start putting money away now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I'd be sixty-three when it lands. Two years short. That's a smaller hole to fill than five, and I think I could make it if I'm careful. But I'd still be the one they push out first, I'm sure of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set myself a target, a year of bills in the building society by 2031, and I'd cut out the meals out and the new car Walter keeps looking at. I'd plan to go at sixty-three on a reduced pension rather than wait to be pushed. And I'd keep working until then, I wouldn't change a thing about how I do the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can do something about. That's different from the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Walter about the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the old one runs and it'll keep running, same as me. He'd grumble and then he'd go and change the oil himself, because that's who he is. We've been married thirty-four years, he knows when I've made my mind up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't change how you do the job. Is there nothing in those five years you'd want to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to teach, if anything. There's a lad on our crew, Owen, nineteen, good hands, and I'd want him to learn the hills properly before the machines come. Where the ground's soft, which farmer's dog bites, which poles were set by the old gang in the sixties and lean if you look at them. If anyone's going to run the robots up there, he should know what they're climbing.

S3.say: I'd still call it a mistake, but with less of a shake in my voice. I'd tell the lads at the depot that five years is time to get their houses in order and start saving now.
S3.think: Privately I think sixty-three is only two years short of my pension, a smaller hole I could fill if I'm careful. I'm still sure I'd be among the first pushed out.
S3.do: Sets a target of a year of bills saved by 2031 and cuts meals out and a planned new car. Plans to leave at sixty-three on a reduced pension rather than wait to be pushed, while working the same way until then.
S3.feel: Worried, but with the sense that it's a worry she can act on.
S3.quote: I'd tell him the old one runs and it'll keep running, same as me.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns Priya's dread into a savings target and a planned exit, so she feels in control even while pressured. She still refuses to change how she works, but wants to pass her local knowledge to a young crew member. That urge to teach is the only forward-looking move she makes toward the new world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's somebody else's problem, I'll be in the choir by then. And then I'd feel bad saying it, because it's my grandchildren's problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For my job, nothing much. I'd be sixty-eight and retired three years. But Daniel's a plumber, and if robots do plumbing then he's forty-five with two teenagers and no trade. And Mark in the army, I don't even want to think about what robots do to soldiering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to sixty-five like I always meant to and keep saving the same. I'd tell Daniel to put something by for the boys' futures and think about whether they should go into a trade at all. I'd vote for whoever says they'll protect working people and keep the depots open, though I don't trust any of them much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Safe for me, but uneasy for the family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your grandsons to do for work, in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know, and that bothers me. I always thought a trade was the safe thing, you can't send a pole repair overseas. Now I'm being told maybe you can't keep it at home either. I'd want them near family and in church, whatever they do, because work can be taken off you but those can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said all along you'd not change how you work. With ten years, does that still hold?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It holds for me. Ten years is enough time for someone like me to finish the way I started, with my own hands. Let the young ones learn the robots. I'll be the old woman at the depot Christmas do telling them how we did it with spikes.

S4.say: I'd say it's somebody else's problem because I'll be singing in the choir by then. Then I'd feel bad, because really it's my grandchildren's problem.
S4.think: Privately I think it barely touches my own job since I'd be long retired. What worries me is my son the plumber at forty-five with no trade, and my other son in the army.
S4.do: Works to sixty-five as planned and keeps saving at the same rate. Urges her son to save for the grandchildren and rethink trades for them, and plans to vote for whoever promises to protect working people and keep rural depots open.
S4.feel: Safe for herself but uneasy for her family.
S4.quote: Work can be taken off you but those can't.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Priya is out before it lands, so her worry moves to her sons and grandchildren. Her belief that a trade is the safest path is shaken, and she has no answer to replace it beyond family and faith. Voting is her one step toward politics, and she takes it with clear distrust of politicians.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Two years and I'm sixty with no pension and no use for the only trade I know. What would help is the company letting people like me take our full pension a few years early if the jobs go, because we've paid in all our lives. Not a handout, what we've earned.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. It won't be anyone in Hollins Cross. It'll be someone in a city office who's never stood under a line in the rain, and they'll call it progress. I'd like those people to come and spend one night on a call-out with us before they decide anything.

headlineQuote: I'd rather go with my pride than stay and be the slow one.
portrait: Priya Rossi is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker who has spent twenty-nine years climbing poles across hill farms from a small rural depot, and was the first woman on her crew. She refuses AI tools, distrusts city managers, and plans to retire at sixty-five and sing in her church choir. She is calm when nothing changes and uneasy about steady change, mainly because she fears the company will close small depots. The two-year AGI picture alarms her: she expects to be pushed out at sixty and would cut spending, retire early and lean on her son rather than the state. With five or ten years she makes a plan she can live with, and her worry moves to her sons and grandchildren.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, which would leave her at sixty with no pension and no use for the only trade she knows.
whatWouldHelp: Letting long-serving workers take their full earned pension a few years early if the jobs disappear, which she sees as earned rather than a handout.
